subject: history_social
passage: Downtown shop owners often oppose raising the price of street parking, fearing that higher prices will drive customers away. Transportation economist Mei-Ling Chen argues the opposite: that higher prices on the busiest blocks free up spaces by discouraging drivers from parking all day, so that more shoppers can find a spot and the shops gain customers.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Chen's argument?

choices.A: After a city raised prices on its busiest downtown blocks, the average parking stay fell by half and shops there reported more customers.
choices.B: Most drivers surveyed said that they would rather pay more for parking than spend time circling the block looking for a space.
choices.C: Shops on blocks where prices were raised reported fewer customers, and many parking spaces sat empty for most of the day.
choices.D: After the price rise, drivers who had parked downtown all day began parking on nearby residential streets and walking the rest of the way.

explanation.why: Chen's argument has a chain: higher prices lead to shorter stays, shorter stays free up spaces, and more shoppers reach the shops. The most direct support reports both ends of the chain after a real price rise: shorter stays and more customers. A finding of fewer customers would support the shop owners instead.
explanation.A: Correct. Shorter stays and more customers after the price rise are exactly the two effects Chen predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. What drivers say they prefer does not show what actually happened to parking turnover or to the shops.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Fewer customers and empty spaces would support the shop owners' fear, not Chen's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Where the all-day parkers went does not show whether shops gained customers.
